article.headline: A Helix in the Browser Reimagines Every Scale of Time
article.lede: Most calendars choose a single granularity and stick to it — month, week, day. A prototype by @codetaur, building on a sketch by @tr_babb, refuses that tradeoff. It renders time as a recursive helix of coils, each nested inside the last, spanning from centuries down to seconds inside a single Three.js/WebGPU scene.
article.body:
The central insight is topological. A linear timeline must scroll; a grid calendar must paginate. A helix can zoom. By stacking coils at decreasing time-scales — centuries wrapping into decades, decades into years, years into days, days into hours, hours into minutes, minutes into seconds — the prototype lets a viewer travel from deep antiquity to a precise timestamp without ever leaving the scene. The OCR from the screenshot shows the interface parked at **-45 BCE, 11/17, 10:04:47**, with the annotation "Augustus becomes Emperor" floating near the relevant coil — proof of concept that historical events can be pinned to a specific moment at any resolution.

The controls visible in the UI (focus coil, spacing, tilt, factor, sec/pixel, transition) suggest the viewer can tune which coil is in focus and how the others cascade around it. This is the recursive part: switching focus from the "decades" coil to the "hours" coil should reorganise the nesting hierarchy rather than simply zooming a flat image.

The renderer is *Three.js* paired with *WebGPU*. Three.js is the dominant JavaScript library for 3D graphics in the browser, abstracting away raw shader code. WebGPU is its emerging substrate — a low-level graphics API that replaces the aging *WebGL* standard, offering near-native GPU performance and compute shaders in the browser. Combining the two places the prototype at the leading edge of what a web page can render, though WebGPU browser support is still partial as of mid-2026.

@codetaur is candid that labels remain rough and credit belongs substantially to @tr_babb's original sketch. That attribution matters: the hard conceptual work — encoding recursive temporal scale as physical coil geometry — appears to precede the implementation. The prototype is a proof that the idea is buildable, not yet a finished instrument.

concepts.definition: A JavaScript library that wraps the browser's 3D graphics pipeline into a friendlier API. Developers describe scenes as objects, lights, and cameras rather than raw GPU instructions. It is the most widely used tool for 3D work in the browser.

The successor to WebGL, the web's older 3D graphics standard. WebGPU gives web applications lower-level, more efficient access to the device GPU — enabling techniques like compute shaders that were impractical on the web before. Browser support is rolling out progressively as of 2025–26.

A visualisation strategy in which time is represented as a spiral or helix, with each coil corresponding to one unit of a given scale (a year, a day, an hour). Nesting multiple coils at different scales inside each other allows a single continuous shape to encode both the very long and the very short without switching views.
